title: Action Recognition vs. Detection + Tracking: When to Use Which
summary: We built action recognition and detection or keypoints + tracking systems for six video tasks, from F1 pit stops to workout reps. Here is when each approach wins.
body_markdown:
*This is a follow-up to*[Train, Evaluate, and Deploy Action Recognition Models with Roboflow](https://roboflow.com/blog/action-recognition) *.*


Action recognition models take a video clip and tell you what happened and when. That's useful, but a lot of video questions can also be answered by running an object detector (or a keypoint model), tracking what it finds, and writing a few rules on top. That setup is cheaper to label and easier to debug, and it also tells you who did what and where.


We wanted to know where the line is, so we built both versions for three tasks: an F1 pit stop, basketball, and workout reps. Then we ran them on the same held-out clips.


F1 pit stop, held-out clip (0.74× speed). Left: detection + tire tracking + rules. Right: action recognition (Cosmos 3 Edge at 8 fps).


**Short version:**


- Action recognition wins when the action is a small movement you can only see across several frames, like a jack lifting a car or a dribble.
- For anything about body pose, like counting reps or telling squats from lunges, a pretrained keypoint model plus a few rules is enough. You don't have to train anything.
- If the question is about objects and places (did something enter a zone, get picked up, get swapped), detection + tracking works well, and you also find out which object and which person.


## What we found


Task Winner Action recognition (F1) Tracking-based (F1)


F1 pit stop Action recognition **62** 49 (detection)


Basketball Action recognition **56** 38 (detection)


Workout reps Keypoints + tracking 56 **96** (keypoints)


*Scores are segment F1 from 0 to 100. A prediction counts if it has the right label and overlaps the real action by at least half.*


For action recognition we trained Cosmos 3 Edge in a Roboflow Action Recognition project. For detection we trained RF-DETR on auto-labeled frames, tracked objects with ByteTrack from the[trackers (opens in a new tab)](https://github.com/roboflow/trackers?ref=blog.roboflow.com) package, and wrote a few dozen lines of rules. For keypoints we used the pretrained RF-DETR keypoint model without any fine-tuning.


## Pit stops: catching the jack


A pit stop has six steps and takes about three seconds. Our footage is shot from above, with a dozen crew members crowded around the car. The hardest part is the jacks. The car goes up a few centimeters, and the lift takes about a quarter of a second.


Our detection + tracking setup didn't catch a single jack step. The car's box barely moves when it's lifted, and the crew blocks the view of the jack. Action recognition missed it at first too, because the model samples video at 4 frames per second by default, so a quarter second is roughly one frame. We retrained the same model at 8 fps, changed nothing else, and it became the best pit stop system overall. In the video above, the 8 fps model catches the jack lift and tracking doesn't.


Tracking was still good at the things boxes can see. For wheel removal, checking whether the original tire is still on the car worked better than action recognition. If we were building this for real, we'd probably use both: tracking for the tires and action recognition for the jacks.


## Basketball: dribbles and made shots


Basketball, held-out test clip (2× speed).


With boxes, you have to write a dribble as a rule, something like "the ball is low and close to a player". That rule hardly ever fired and caught 1 of 5 dribbles. Shots were tricky too. A made shot means the ball goes through the rim from above, but the ball is small and blurry, and when the detector loses it in the net, a make gets counted as a miss.


Action recognition doesn't need to find the ball or the rim at all. It just learns what a dribble or a made shot looks like, and it caught all 5 dribbles. It needed only 13 training examples to learn made shots.


## Workouts: just use keypoints


Lunges with keypoints + tracking, held-out test clip.


If the action is something your body does, you probably don't need to train a model. A pretrained keypoint model gives you 17 points per person, and from there each exercise is a few lines of geometry:


- **Push-up:** the torso tilts more than 40° from vertical.
- **Jumping jack:** the wrists go above the shoulders.
- **Squat or lunge:** count each time the hips dip. If the knees are at different heights at the bottom of the dip, it's a lunge.


Those rules counted every rep with zero training. Action recognition was almost perfect at saying which exercise someone was doing, but it merged ten jumping jacks into one long segment, so it can't count reps on its own. Plain person boxes didn't work either, since a box looks about the same for a squat and a lunge.


## A few tips


If you go with **action recognition** , label enough clips (dozens per action, not a handful). Raise the frame rate (video sampling rate) if an action lasts a second or less, and add a counter on top if you need reps.


If you go with **detection + tracking** , make sure your model can actually see what matters. For squats vs. lunges that means keypoints, not boxes. Detector accuracy is also very important, as tracking won't be robust if your detections are flickering.
